default.note: The shipped field battle: Campus Martius, ultra order of battle, quality=high, 8,632 men. Recorded at 88a4aa5. Re-record only in the same commit as the change that moved it. ||| Re-recorded by the determinism-cliff pass, and this one is a re-record of the FORMAT rather than of the battle. Two things changed. (1) Two checkpoints added past t+200: the gate used to stop 5.5 s before the only cross-engine divergence anyone has measured (the field battle forks at t+205.5 s), so t+250 is the sentinel just past the fork and t+400 is the second half of the battle nothing had ever looked at. (2) Two new marks per checkpoint. `uf64` is the exact float64 bits of every continuous UnitGroupState field plus the waypoint queue — the layer the float32 pool hash cannot see, and which nothing in this repository hashed until now. `uctl` is the discrete half: order, target, formation, width, alive, kills, membership, flags, and unit array order. The five original pool hashes are UNCHANGED at all three battles across the whole pass, including across the Math.hypot -> Math.sqrt(a*a + b*b) substitution in the same branch, and so are all 21 survivor counts. Every `uf64` moved, and no `uctl` did: the substitution perturbs the simulation own float64 state everywhere, never reaches a control-flow decision, and never survives the float32 round trip. That is the quantisation firewall, and it is why the old five-checkpoint pool-only gate would have reported that a 222-call-site change did nothing. A `uf64` drift with `hash` and `uctl` unchanged is a PORTABILITY finding — a browser update is enough to cause one — and the gate warns rather than fails on it. A `uctl` or `hash` drift is a real change in the battle and still fails. Recorded from three independent page loads per battle, cross-checked against an earlier independent pair of runs: all 21 checkpoints reproduced exactly. Headcounts 8,632 / 3,074 / 3,440 confirm each arm measured the battle it names. ||| Re-recorded by the pass that put the field deployment on its own ground, and this one IS a re-record of the battle. `sim/scenario.ts` laid both lines out about x 0 and never read the deployment masks; §15 task 1 moved those masks east with the corrected Tiber and left the order of battle where it was, so at 70fc191 **747 of these 8,632 men were standing in the river** and another 412 were dry on the far bank, in the wrong battle. Measured with `tools/probe-ground.mjs --quality=high --views=none`, which now audits the men as well as the ground. The deployment is now translated once onto the axis the masks define — one shift of 271.146 m for every unit of both armies, so frontage (Rome 684.3 m, the host 783.4 m), spacing, width, facing, formation, unit count and headcount are identical to the metre before and after; only x moved. In water 747 -> 0, far bank 412 -> 0, worst slope under a man 0.529 -> 0.315. The battle that follows is a different battle for the obvious reason: an army that was fighting with its left wing in a river is not the same army. Survivors at t+400 move 5,217 -> 4,288. The previous pin was already red at 70fc191 for a different reason — the terrain pass at c44ded0 moved the ground under this battle and deliberately did not re-record it, on the grounds that pinning it would pin a broken battle. Measured at 70fc191 in a separate worktree, for the record: t+0 0fa6e702, then ee0f62b6, d343cc70, 3d79f110, 8ebc59fe, 7b951be2, 233e3022. Recorded from three independent page loads, all bit-identical at all seven checkpoints on hash, uf64 and uctl. One mark says the composition claim better than any prose can: **`uctl` at t+0 is 2b2ac282 and at t+30 is 13f5b86e, which are the values recorded at 88a4aa5**, before the terrain moved and before this. The discrete half — order, target, formation, width, alive, kills, membership, flags and unit array order — is byte-identical to the battle that shipped. Only the continuous half moved, and only in x. ||| **Re-recorded by §15 task 14's box widening, which is the change that moved it.** The owner's decision was that *battle lines should fit their deployment boxes* and that the boxes should be *widened east*; unit composition, strengths and counts were not touched, and the frontages are the same to the metre (Rome 684.3 m, the host 783.4 m). Three things moved. (1) Both boxes were widened east with their **west edges pinned exactly where task 1 measured them against the Tiber** — the attacker's half-width 380 → 515 about cx 205 → 340, the defender's 250 → 425 about 205 → 380. (2) `standOnDeploymentGround` now insets its west anchor by the box's own feather, because the rectangle's edge is the contour where the mask reaches *zero*; that is 80 m of eastward shift, 271.146 → 351.146, one number for every unit of both armies. (3) `battleCoreMask` came off x 0 onto the deployment axis at a 745 m half-width, so the host's right wing is inside the damped corridor for the first time since task 1 (440 men were outside it). Measured by `tools/probe-ground.mjs --quality=high`: men outside their own box **562 Roman and 182 Juthungi → 0 and 0**, trees within 4 m of a man 1/4 → 0/0, worst slope under a man 0.315/0.048 → 0.074/0.076, in water 0 → 0, far bank 0 → 0. Survivors at t+400 move 4,288 → 4,660, which is what a battle fought on prepared instead of unprepared ground does. **The control is Carthage**, not this arm: `map=carthage&scenario=assault` is bit-identical across this tree at all seven checkpoints on `hash`, `uf64` and `uctl` at 3,440 men, and the shift on Carthage and on Pydna is still exactly 0.000 m (`tools/scratch/probe-standshift.mjs`). Worth writing down because the instruction for this pass got it the other way round: **`default` IS the Campus Martius field battle**, so it can never be a control for a change to that battle's deployment. A and B agree on every bit at all seven checkpoints here. One mark carries the whole "this is positioning, not balance" claim: **`uctl` at t+0 is still `2b2ac282`**, the value recorded at `88a4aa5` before the Tiber moved and before task 1 — the discrete half of every unit (order, target, formation, width, alive, kills, membership, flags, unit array order) is byte-identical to the battle that shipped. Only the continuous half moved, and only in x, for the second time. ||| **Correction, 3 Sep 2026, from a review: the `3,074` in the historical segments above is stale prose, not a stale pin.** Rome's assault has been **3,072** since the order of battle lost one squadron of horse and gained one great warband (`docs/HANDOFF.md`); those segments were written before it and are kept as written, because this note is a log rather than a description. The headcount tells are **8,632 / 3,072 / 3,440**, and the pins in this file were correct throughout — only the sentence about them was not. ||| **Re-recorded by the about-face pass, and this one IS a re-record of the battle.** Three things about a body of men changing which way it points were wrong at once, and the owner reported two of them: "my friend was trying to control the cavalry but they kept running away — they were not routed, but they would not turn around to face", and "there is no way for a unit to 'about face'... instead the entire unit rotates". (1) `p.slot[i]` was written at birth and never again — two writers in the whole tree, both in a spawn path — so a facing change rotated every slot's world position and left every man bound to the slot he was born in; and because the anchor is the middle of the *front rank* rather than the middle of the block, the rotation also threw the whole body forward by its own depth. (2) `integrate` wrote a man's heading in exactly one place, guarded by `speed > 0.22`, so a man who was not walking never turned and a formation could not come to face a new direction without marching. (3) The standing wheel ran at 0.6 rad/s — five seconds for a half turn — during all of which every man chased a slot that was somewhere else. `src/sim/reform.ts` re-solves which man holds which slot when the shape moves out from under them, `pivotAboutCentre` turns a standing block about its own footprint, `turningInPlace` holds its men still while it turns, and the wheel now runs at the men's own turn rate. Measured with `tools/probe-aboutface.mjs` on a 160-man legionary cohort at ease ordered to about-face: median travel **20.45 -> 1.63 m**, men who ended up further from where they stood than half their own unit is wide **92/160 -> 14/160**, bearing error thirty seconds later **75.6 -> 2.1 degrees**, and the block's own along-facing extent -5.21..0.10 -> -0.16..5.28 before against -5.21..0.10 -> -5.21..0.18 after. Sixty Roman cavalry: **27.50 -> 1.35 m** and **0 of 60** across their own block. A real squadron of the shipped field battle, in wedge, with only the two AIs silenced so the order under test is the only order it has: **48.28 -> 3.24 m** and 126.4 -> 2.1 degrees. **What did not move, which is the confinement.** `t+0` is byte-identical on `hash`, `uf64` and `uctl` in all three battles, so the order of battle, the deployment, and every unit's width, formation, facing and position at the start are exactly what shipped. On the field battle `uctl` at `t+30` is still `13f5b86e`, the value recorded at `88a4aa5`: thirty seconds in, the discrete half of every unit — order, target, formation, width, alive, kills, membership, flags and unit array order — is unchanged and only the continuous half has moved. Headcounts are unchanged at 8,632 / 3,072 / 3,440, and all four quality tiers still produce the identical battle, which is the constraint that whatever this does it must not be a graphics setting. A and B agree on every bit at all seven checkpoints in all three battles. **Survivors do move from `t+90` on, and that is the change rather than a side effect of it.** Men who stand in different places and face the way they were told are in reach of different men; and `p.rank`, which `Combat` reads to decide who is eager to join a melee and `Projectiles` to decide who may shoot over whom, is derived from the slot and now tracks it instead of being frozen at spawn. At `t+400`: field battle 5,615 -> 5,132, Rome's assault 2,242 -> 1,973, Carthage 2,412 -> 2,368. Recorded from run A of a run whose A and B were bit-identical at all seven checkpoints. ||| Re-recorded by the horse-rear pass, and the whole of the reason is one line of `Combat.fightUnits`. `impacted` — "this horseman has spent his charge impact" — was cleared the instant he had no target, which in a melee is one tick, and the trample manufactures that tick itself: it shoves the victim away at 2.4 m/s and brakes the horse to 0.35, so the pair leave KEEP_PAD, the target drops, and he re-acquires on his next striped tick and tramples again. Measured on the shipped field battle at a0908f1: 4,432 trample impacts in four minutes, 86.6 % of them repeats, median gap between one man’s own impacts 0.27 s — the eight-tick acquisition stripe exactly — and 91.6 % running on the Math.max(chargeF, 0.35) floor. `TRAMPLE_REARM_TICKS` now makes a horseman be continuously clear of any opponent for 30 * CONTACT_RELEASE (2.5 s) before his horse hits like a horse again; the first impact of a charge is untouched. Impacts fall to 2,162, mounted men entering Staggered from 1,568 to 668, and cavalry alive at t+240 rises from 115 of 660 to 346 — cavalry were not fighting, they were trampling. So fewer men die and the survivors stand elsewhere. THE CONFINEMENT IS THE INTERESTING PART AND IT IS MEASURED: every battle is bit-identical to its old pin until its own cavalry make contact and drifts at the first checkpoint after that and not before — the field battle and Rome’s assault unchanged at t+0 and t+30, Carthage’s unchanged at t+0, t+30, t+90, t+150 AND t+200, because its cavalry are the last on the field to engage. A vs B identical at every checkpoint on all three, and all four quality tiers identical on all three in the verification pass immediately before this one (the record pass itself ran --tiers=off, so its own CROSS-TIER SKIPPED line is expected and is not the tier evidence). The renderer’s REAR_EDGE, which stops a stationary rear clip playing on a horse travelling faster than a trot, is render-only and is the reason the tier arm matters here.
